title: Translations are not always accurate
text:
I would probably have given this app three or four stars, however, there are lots of inaccuracies in the translations. For instance, the same Italian phrase for “do you want some beer?” and “do you want to drink some beer?” obviously these two sentences are not the same, in neither English nor Italian. Obviously the meaning is very, very similar, but when learning a language the distinction is important.

Another flaw with the app is the inability to slow down or speed up the flow of speech. It would be nice to be able to have a little more time for talking. Of course the workaround is simply pause the app, but one of the selling points is you can listen while you’re doing other things, which of course means it’s hard to stop what you’re doing to pause the app. A bit of a Catch-22.

There are some really good things about the app, the main one being the lessons focus on learning how to actually carry on a conversation, rather than concerns with conjugating verbs, etc. Although both are important there is something to be said for being able to actually carry on a simple conversation.

Unfortunately, the inaccuracies are a dealbreaker for me and I won’t be renewing after my free period is finished.

title: One obvious flaw
text:
I am using this app specifically to make learning in the car possible. But every time I try to access this app through CarPlay it says “open this app on your phone.”  So the app works in the car, but only if you manually unlock your phone and open it first, which goes a long way towards negating the point. 

In terms of content, I first did Pimsleur through audible. I thought it was very overpriced through audible and not so easy to navigate. But the app isn’t a ton better—for me, when the menu opens in CarPlay it doesn’t say which lesson I left off on—I have to remember. It’s still pricey to use this. I also think the Pimsleur courses have some dated phrasing in terms of formality. 

But I haven’t found a better option for car learning, so here I be.

title: ⭐ 1/5 — Congratulations, Pimsleur. You Finally Got the Review You Wouldn’t Stop Asking For.
text:
⭐ 1/5 — Congratulations, Pimsleur. You Finally Got the Review You Wouldn’t Stop Asking For.

Pimsleur has managed to accomplish something remarkable: take an otherwise excellent language-learning application and make me actively resent opening it.

The lessons are good. The methodology works. I genuinely enjoy the educational content. Unfortunately, someone on the product development team apparently decided that repeatedly interrupting paying customers to beg for App Store reviews was an acceptable substitute for respecting their time.

Every time I open this application, my intention is simple: to learn a language, not to participate in your marketing campaign.

Yet the relentless review prompts continue. There appears to be no meaningful option to say, “I like your application, but I do not wish to leave a review. Please stop asking.”

Apparently, declining isn’t an answer. It’s merely an invitation to be harassed again later.

The irony is extraordinary. You have a customer who enjoys your product, voluntarily returns to use it, and is willing to pay for the service. Rather than leave that customer alone to learn, you repeatedly interrupt the experience until you’ve converted genuine satisfaction into outright frustration.

So congratulations, Pimsleur. Your persistence has paid off.

You wanted a review badly enough to repeatedly disrupt the very experience I’m paying you to provide. Here it is: one star.

Not because your language instruction deserves it, but because your complete disregard for the customer’s attention, autonomy, and repeated refusal deserves public criticism.

Here’s a revolutionary product-design suggestion: When a customer declines to review your application, respect the decision and stop asking.

I paid to learn a language. I did not pay to be relentlessly solicited for free advertising.

You didn’t earn this review through excellence. You extracted it through irritation.

title: Disappointing
text: The 30 minute lessons are impractical for people who have 15 minutes at a time. There is no assessment of your skill level and feedback is minimal. In today’s Duolingo world, a 50 year old strategy of flash cards and self learning is disappointing. Don’t make the mistake of subscribing if you aren’t committed. Chose a month by month plan to start with. They offer zero refunds. Just a greedy old business with a long history in the language learning space.

title: Speechless!
text: I downloaded this app not because I chose to, but because YouTube’s Pimsleur ad, “juggling fire.. (weird)” curtailed my ability to “skip ad” button watching something really really important.  I was literally forced into the Apple App Store pressing “download” and took merrily two seconds to realize I would never in my life use this app, why am I here??, I didn’t want the Pimsleur app to begin with!  I’ve now lost, nor can I remember the video I was watching that this ad had taken me away from...  So for that, I give it one star.  Youtube should always be ad free IMO, if not, at least keep “skip ad” buttons in clear view, not half overlaying “install now” ad buttons all over it!

text: I really like way too long, especially every day. I wish I could break it down to 15 seconds. That’s about all my attention span can handle and why I end up using Duolingo a lot more

title: Not useful
text: I bought this hoping to learn learn some Swiss German. For that, this app is not helpful to me at all! It does not start with any basics, like sounds of letters etc. The phrases it makes you learn and practice are not at all useful for travel or everyday basics. I would love to pick through the flashcards to learn some words that would be helpful, but it won’t let you do anything if you haven’t completed the very boring and unhelpful lessons. It’s terrible. Waste of time and money

title: Poor UI, dull,
text: simple tasks, like trying a language, once selected it is impossible to unselect: app dev 101. Lessons are boring and too slow (at least for languages related to native language). Maybe ok for very different languages. Also should evaluate current knowledge and suggest a starting point. This is possible if they're already using voice AI.

title: Not recommended for Japanese
text: 1 star because I liked that you can listen to 30 minute lessons while stuck in morning and afternoon traffic. The multiple choice quiz questions are useless because there is always 1 obvious correct choice. You aren’t going to learn any hiragana or reading relying on their reading lessons which are done poorly. The order in which you learn things is nonsensical. It was well over 30 lessons before you learn things like “nice to meet you”. But one of the first things you learn is that you would like to buy gloves and a keychain? After 60 lessons I think I still didn’t learn how to ask for the check at a restaurant.
